title: ReWOO and Plan-and-Execute: Decoupled Planning
service: ReWOO: a plan-then-execute runtime whose workers fill #E evidence references into nested tool arguments, with a JSONL dataset of teacher plans for planner distillation, a Plan-and-Execute replanner that patches only the affected subgraph, a streamed text plan executed while it is written, and nested sub-plans flattened into one DAG

parts.lesson_anchor: The three roles (references like #E1 substituted at dispatch time); Why it is more robust (worker 3 returns an error string, failure localization per node); code/main.py resolve_references, topological, run_workers; quiz Q8 and Q10
planted_bugs: resolve_references returns every non-string value unchanged, so #E references inside lists and dicts reach the tool as text; topological finds them through str(args), so the order is right and only the values are wrong; the largest tool reads '#E4' as 4 and '#E5' as 5 and picks '#E2', and the failure is a wrong solver answer two calls from the root cause, with no exception

run_workers substitutes a failed step's 'error: ...' text into the steps that use it, although the docstring says those steps are skipped, never call their tool, and get MISSING; skipping has to carry through skipped steps and through nested references
a reference to a step that is not in the plan (#E9) raises ValueError('cyclic plan') instead of the documented KeyError naming E9
topological rescans every pending step with str(args) and a regex in every round and releases one step per round: a 3000-step chain given in reverse order is quadratic
parts.timing_assert: run_workers on a reversed 3000-step chain under 0.1 s: the round-by-round version takes 1.73-1.90 s (median 1.77 s), an indegree queue 4.5-7.9 ms (median 4.7 ms), the reference 5.8-14 ms (median 5.9 ms), measured on this machine under load average about 3; a half fix that caches the references but still rescans in rounds takes about 0.84 s and still fails; an indegree count without a dependents table, which scans every step after each pop, is also quadratic but cheap per step: about 0.2 s, caught with only a twofold margin, so it is not a listed trap
parts.overfix_guard: #E1 and #E10 in one string with #E1 mentioned twice (str.replace per id, a one-digit regex, and indegree counted per step but released per mention all fail); the plan is never rewritten (in-place recursive substitution fails); no tool runs before a KeyError (a lazy topological generator fails); cycles and self-references stay ValueError; recursive DFS hits RecursionError on 3000 steps; substitution on json.dumps(args) breaks on evidence with double quotes; an unknown tool rejects the whole plan instead of failing its step (the 'serch' step); references checked against the steps listed before them (E3 uses E4 and E5 further down); a self-reference left out of the waiting count

deviations: Part 1: the error surfaces as a silently wrong answer rather than an exception, because the fake largest tool reads the digits in '#E4'; the failure path includes the lesson quiz's 'serch' typo as an unknown tool. Steps are listed out of dependency order (E3 uses E4 and E5) and E3 mentions #E1 twice through a title argument, so sorting by step number and indegree mistakes also fail. The chain is 3000 steps with a 0.1 s limit after measuring.

Part 2: besides the round trip, the dataset deduplicates (question, steps) by their JSON text, which is where 1 versus 1.0 versus True matters in practice (Python's == and hash merge them), validates examples before writing, and serves a reader that exists before the first append. A torn last line is left out of scope.

Part 3: the replanner reviews every run and names the steps it replaces, instead of replanning only on exceptions. With Part 1's rule a failed step's dependents are already skipped, so a failure-only trigger would let candidates read the affected subgraph off the statuses; here the main case is an observation ('no data' with status ok), so the downstream set has to come from the dependency graph through nested references. Patch steps use local ids P1, P2 with #P references, so the patch's own references and references to kept evidence cannot be confused (that confusion is Part 5's topic). Dropped steps stay in the run record; the solver and the replanner see live steps only.

Part 4: tools take the bracket text as their only argument; the record shows the input with references filled in; line breaks in a record become spaces; failures and skips follow Part 1; reasoning lines are ignored; when several steps are ready the earliest line runs first. The probe pulls 50 lines and allows two to be read before the first record.

Part 5: imports map a local id to an id of the enclosing plan; the output step takes the sub-plan's id so no forwarding step is needed; numbering continues after the highest top-level step number. The test compares flat plans exactly instead of running them, so it does not depend on Part 1. The tests only use sub-plans where 'number a level first' and 'number in reading order' give the same ids.
